idiom_name: didSet observer that nils the cached optional
implementation_notes: Property observers are the invalidation hook: the cached derived value lives in a private optional and every source property's didSet (or willSet) clears it, so marking happens in exactly one place per source and cannot be forgotten at call sites. The accessor is a computed property that rebuilds when the slot is empty; in a struct it needs `mutating get`, which means a let instance cannot trigger the first build, so classes are the easier host when the cache is shared. Swift's `lazy var` is the one-shot cousin - it computes on first access and never again - so it replaces lazy initialisation, not this pattern; the classic structure is justified when the computed value is expensive and the source mutates more often than the value is read.
pitfalls: didSet runs only for assignments to the property itself; mutating a reference-type member or an element of a class-based collection never fires it, so invalidate from the owning method.
Observers are not called during initialisation (assignments in init skip didSet), so the initial state must already be dirty - nil cache or true flag.
A `lazy var` cache cannot be invalidated and requires var (not let), so it is unavailable to immutable value types and to the invalidation use case.

`mutating get` in a struct means a let-bound instance cannot rebuild the cache (compile error) and thread-shared value types lose exclusivity - decide between value and reference semantics deliberately.

variants.name: Property wrapper that owns the dirty slot
variants.implementation_notes: A property wrapper packages the flag and the cache into one declaration: the wrappedValue getter rebuilds when its slot is empty and the setter clears the slot, so the pattern appears as `@Dirty(build: ...) var world: World` and invalidation is expressed by writing the property. Since the wrapper's storage is a stored property, its getter must be `mutating`, which restricts wrappers to structs' mutating contexts or classes. Swift's initialisation rules also matter: a property-wrapper initialiser cannot capture `self`, so the builder closure must be constructed from outside the instance (or the wrapper must take a key path), which limits how naturally it fits per-instance caches.
pitfalls: A wrapper initialiser cannot reference `self`, so the build closure cannot read the instance it belongs to - pass a key path or build the wrapper outside the type.
The wrapper's documentation/limits: wrappedValue needs `mutating get` for struct storage, so a let instance cannot trigger a rebuild, and class storage pays a reference indirection.
Property wrappers are partial in the language: they cannot be applied to `let` properties, to closures stored with @escaping semantics in every position, or to top-level globals in the same way.
Overriding a wrapped property or accessing `$world` (the projected value) changes semantics: the projected value exposes the wrapper, so keeping it private avoids callers clearing the cache directly.
